name: ADM3053BRWZ-REEL7
title: ADM3053: CAN transceiver with signal and power isolation and a built-in isolated DC-to-DC converter, 2.5 kV rms, 20-lead SOIC_W
summary: A complete isolated CAN node interface in one wide-body SOIC: a two-channel digital isolator, an ISO 11898 CAN transceiver and an isoPower DC-to-DC converter that makes the bus-side 5 V from the logic-side 5 V supply. The logic interface (TxD, RxD) runs from VIO of 3.3 V or 5 V; the converter takes 4.5 V to 5.5 V on VCC. Data rates reach 1 Mbps, a resistor on RS sets slope control for lower emissions, and the driver is protected by current limiting and thermal shutdown. The barrier is rated 2500 V rms for one minute (UL 1577) with VIORM 560 V peak.

circuits.title: Example isolated CAN node
circuits.description: The ADM3053 between a CAN controller and a two-wire bus connector. A 5 V supply feeds VCC, decoupled by 10 µF and 100 nF to GND1; a 3.3 V or 5 V supply feeds both the controller and VIO, decoupled by 10 nF and 100 nF. The controller's TxD and RxD go straight to the pins of the same names. On the bus side VISOOUT is wired to VISOIN, with 100 nF and 10 µF at VISOOUT and 100 nF and 10 nF at VISOIN, all to GND2. A resistor RS from the RS pin to GND2 sets the slope, RT terminates the bus across CANH and CANL at the connector, and VREF is left open. GND1 and GND2 are separate grounds on either side of the barrier.

parts.note: slope resistor; 0 Ω or a short to GND2 for high-speed mode

RL loads the bus across CANH and CANL (60 Ω in the supply-current rows), RS runs from the RS pin to GND2 (RS low in those rows), and VREF is open.

equations.note: The decoder threshold is about 0.5 V and the transformer pulses exceed 1.0 V. The allowed field is set so the induced voltage stays at or below half of that 0.5 V margin; at 1 MHz, 0.2 kgauss induces 0.25 V. Arriving during a transmitted pulse with the worst-case polarity, that voltage cuts the received pulse from over 1.0 V to 0.75 V.

operation.text: Three blocks share the package: an isoPower DC-to-DC converter, a two-channel iCoupler digital isolator, and a CAN transceiver meeting ISO 11898. An on-chip oscillator drives an internal transformer with a pair of square waves to carry power across the barrier, so a single 5 V supply powers the whole isolated node. Unpowered nodes leave the bus undisturbed, and 110 or more nodes can share one bus.

The bus is dominant when CANH − CANL exceeds 0.9 V and recessive when it is below 0.5 V. Dominant: the driver pulls CANH high and CANL low. Recessive: both outputs are high impedance. TxD low gives dominant; TxD high or floating gives recessive. With VIO off the bus stays recessive; with VCC off the driver state is indeterminate. RxD goes high with open inputs or with VCC off.

RS (pin 18) picks the mode. Tied to ground, the output transistors switch as fast as they can with no edge limiting (high-speed mode); a shielded bus cable is advised in this mode to keep emissions down. With a resistor from RS to ground the edges are slowed (slope-control mode), which allows unshielded twisted-pair or parallel-wire bus lines. The edge rate follows the current drawn out of RS: ISLOPE −10 µA to −200 µA with RS at 1.8 V to 3.3 V. At RS = 47 kΩ the bus slew rate is 7 V/µs typ.

Isolation sits on the logic side. TxD, referred to GND1, crosses the barrier to the transceiver, referred to GND2; the receiver output comes back the other way to RxD on GND1. VIO powers the signal channels, which lets the logic interface run at 3.3 V or 5 V.

The converter uses secondary-side control with isolated PWM feedback. VCC powers an oscillator whose current drives a small air-core transformer built on the chip; the bus side rectifies and regulates the result to 5 V. The bus-side controller sends a PWM signal back to the VCC side over its own iCoupler channel, and that signal modulates the oscillator to set how much power crosses. Its oscillator runs at 180 MHz.
Driver outputs are current limited. If a short to a stiff source heats the die to 150°C, the thermal circuit turns the driver outputs off; they come back on when the die has cooled to 140°C.

Each logic edge at an isolator input sends a pulse of about 1 ns through the transformer to a bistable decoder. If the input has not changed for more than 1 µs, refresh pulses carrying the present state are sent. If the decoder sees no pulses for about 5 µs it treats the input side as unpowered and a watchdog forces the output to its default state; this should happen only at power-up and power-down.

The 3.3 V operating condition is the most susceptible. Only very large currents at high frequency close to the part disturb it: at 1 MHz a 0.5 kA current would have to be 5 mm away. Strong high-frequency fields can still induce error voltages in loops formed by board traces, so those loops need care in layout.

Each supply pin needs a small low-inductance capacitor for noise and a large one for ripple and regulation: VIO (pin 6) to GND1, 100 nF and 10 nF; VCC (pin 8) to GND1 (pin 9), 100 nF and 10 µF; VISOOUT (pin 12) to GND2 (pin 11), 100 nF and 10 µF; VISOIN (pin 19) to GND2 (pin 20), 100 nF and 10 nF. The smaller value should be a very low inductance ceramic part, and the total lead length from both capacitor ends to the supply pin is at most 10 mm. VISOOUT and VISOIN must be joined on the board. The data channels also put switching transients on the supply pins.

The part dissipates about 650 mW at full load and cannot take a heat sink; heat leaves through the ground pins into the board. At high ambient temperature give the ground pins a thermal path to the ground plane: enlarged pads on pins 1, 3, 9, 10, 11, 14, 16 and 20 with several vias each to the plane. Pad size is the designer's choice, set by board space.

Keep coupling across the barrier on the board small, and lay out so that whatever coupling remains reaches all pins on one side of the part equally. Otherwise fast common-mode transients can push pins past their absolute maximum ratings and cause latch-up or damage.

The converter's very high switching frequency puts high-frequency currents into board ground and power planes, which radiate from edges and as dipoles. A grounded enclosure is advised; without one, RF layout practice applies to the board.

Insulation wears out under long voltage stress, at a rate set by the waveform across it. Bipolar AC is the hardest case, and its 50-year lifetime sets the recommended working voltage of 424 V peak. Unipolar AC (swinging between 0 V and a limit of either sign, never crossing 0 V) and DC stress the insulation much less, so the higher working voltages in the continuous working voltage table apply to them while keeping a 50-year life. A waveform fitting neither case is treated as bipolar AC. Running above the lifetime voltage shortens the insulation's life.
